title: POC hosting decision scoping - Tidewave Systems
summary: Discovery / POC scoping to decide between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Key topics: success criteria (latency < 120ms p50, cost targets), workload sizing (avg 800 qps daily, spiky peak 6k qps for 2 hours), benchmark plan (end-to-end latency + cold-start + KV cache hit scenarios), data residency and encryption requirements, timeline aiming for 6-week pilot. Next steps: Redwood to share pilot SOW, benchmark spreadsheet, and a cost-comparison matrix; Tidewave to provide sample traffic profile and representative model weights or reference model; schedule bench run week of 2025-03-31.

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-03-19
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Ellis (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (Redwood SA), Alex Rivera (Tidewave CTO), Mei Chen (Lead MLE), David Ortiz (Cloud Ops), Sophie Liao (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
- Discussion of POC scope and decision criteria between hosted, dedicated and private deployments.
- Agreed to run hosted baseline benchmarks, then evaluate dedicated reserved capacity for predictable throughput, and runway to private (VPC/on-prem) if compliance required.

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining — can we do quick intros? I'm Jordan Ellis, account lead. Samira and Priya from our side will cover the technical bits.
[00:18] Alex (Tidewave CTO): Alex here. Quick context — Tidewave runs a conversational commerce assistant embedded in our mobile app; our throughput is steady with pronounced spikes during promo windows. We're exploring a POC to decide which inference deployment mode makes sense.
[00:35] Sophie (PM): We need clear success criteria end to end — latency and cost are the two big ones for execs.
[00:42] Samira (Redwood SE): Absolutely. We're hoping to nail down p50/p95 latency targets, cost per 1M tokens, and what model compatibility looks like (LLM family, quantization).
[00:58] Mei (Lead MLE): To be concrete: our current internal infra has p50 ~95ms for a distilled 8B. We expect to move to a 13B or 70B for improved quality. We care about cold start behavior for rare heavy tails too.
[01:20] Jordan: Great. Quick high level on options: Hosted is fastest to start and low ops, Dedicated gives you reserved GPUs for predictable throughput and cost, Private gives you full control for compliance (VPC or on-prem). Each has tradeoffs.
[01:41] David (Cloud Ops): On compliance — we have customers in EU that require data residency and we use customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest. Is that supported?
[01:50] Priya (Redwood SA): Yes, our Private option supports customer KMS/HSM and VPC peering; Dedicated can also be provisioned in region and integrate with key management depending on contract. Hosted supports tenant encryption and specific region deployments but not customer-managed HSM unless in Dedicated/Private.
[02:12] Alex: OK that's useful. Can you outline a POC plan including what benchmarks you would run and what we need to provide?
[02:20] Samira: We'll scope a two-phase POC. Phase 1: Hosted baseline — verify latency & cost with your representative workload. Phase 2: Dedicated sizing and stress tests — validate scaling, warm vs cold cache, and cost delta. Phase 3 optional: Private proof-of-concept for compliance-sensitive flows.
[02:38] Mei: For the hosted baseline, what's the setup time? We have a week to get initial numbers.
[02:44] Jordan: Hosted baseline can be stand-up in 2 business days once we have access and traffic sample; benchmark run could be done end of next week.
[02:52] [Background cough]
[03:05] Sophie: Success criteria — can we put numbers on it now? Exec target is p50 < 120ms and p95 < 400ms for typical user prompts, and cost per 1M tokens < $X (TBD by finance).
[03:22] Samira: p50 < 120ms is realistic for a 13B with optimized runtime under Redwood Dedicated with warm KV cache; hosted baseline for 13B might hit p50 in 100-180ms depending on payload. p95 will be higher — we should run percentile breakdown per sequence length.
[03:42] Mei: Important: many of our prompts include multi-node context and tool calls; KV cache hit rate will swing effective latency.
[03:54] Priya: We'll include KV cache scenarios in the benchmark spreadsheet: cold start, warm cache, and prefix cache hit ratios at 10/50/90%.
[04:08] Alex: Workload sizing: our telemetry shows average concurrent qps ~30 sustained (which maps to ~800 qps daily across time zones?) — sorry I'm mixing units. Let me give a short doc after the call. Peak during promos we've seen spikes up to 6k qps for ~2 hours.
[04:28] Jordan: That's exactly the sort of tail we need to simulate. For Dedicated we size based on 99th percentile routing and autoscale bursts. We'll propose capacity with burst pool to handle the promo.
[04:40] David: On autoscaling, how fast is warm-up? Do you rely on cold-starts for new model instances?
[04:46] Samira: Our runtime supports continuous batching and fast KV cache population; cold-start can be mitigated via pre-warmed instances or keeping a min-replica. For Dedicated we can reserve additional idle GPUs or use burst capacity. For Hosted, burst behavior depends on available pool and tier.
[05:05] Alex: Are there any hidden costs for cache warming or pre-warmed capacity? Finance wants predictability.
[05:12] Jordan: We'll include cost of reserved GPUs and a model for cost per token with and without warm replicas. The cost matrix will show hosted per-token price, dedicated reserved cost amortized, and projected Private infra op-ex.
[05:28] Mei: Regarding model size — you mentioned running 70B as an option; what does that do to latency and hardware needs?
[05:34] Priya: 70B needs beefier GPUs and typically yields higher latency; quantization can help. For 70B we recommend Dedicated or Private for predictable throughput; hosted can still run it but may have more variance and cost. We'll include quantization recommendations in Optimize notes.
[05:54] Sophie: Security checklist — SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, and SOC2 assurances. We want to know what evidence you can provide for compliance.
[06:03] Priya: We have SOC 2 and ISO documents we can share and an enterprise security pack: audit logs, per-request audit IDs, role-based controls, and SAML SSO integrations. For Private we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM.
[06:20] Alex: Good. Also need to know data retention policy for logs and whether training data could see user data — we are strict.
[06:28] Samira: Redwood does not use customer data for model training in hosted or dedicated unless explicitly contracted for analytics; logs retention can be configured and we can scrub PII in transit. We'll provide the privacy whitepaper.
[06:44] [08:00] Jordan: Let's walk through the benchmark plan — Samira, want to describe the tests you'll run?
[08:05] Samira: Sure. We'll run: 1) Single-request latency matrix across seq lengths (16/64/256 tokens), 2) End-to-end p50/p95 under steady state (sustained 800 qps equivalent), 3) Spike test with ramp to 6k qps for 2-hour window, 4) Cold-start behavior with instance spin-up, 5) KV/prefix cache hit scenarios and token cost breakdown. We'll also capture tail latency and token throughput.
[08:34] Mei: For the steady-state test, can you mimic our mix of generation + tool calls? About 30% of the requests call an external tool.
[08:41] Samira: Yes, capture external tool latency as a simulated stub or a real call if you provide an endpoint. We'll include tool call latency in the benchmark so you see end-to-end.
[08:52] Sophie: How will you measure cost for Hosted vs Dedicated? We want real-world per-token dollars including infra overhead and bandwidth.
[08:59] Jordan: We'll produce a cost model: hosted per-token pricing (what you'd pay on Redwood API), dedicated amortized GPU cost + software fee + expected per-token runtime cost, and private infra op-ex estimates (capex and ops). We'll include a sensitivity analysis for cache hit rates.
[09:17] David: Who on our side needs to be involved during bench runs? Cloud ops will need to give network access if we call internal services and our security team may want to be on the call.
[09:26] Jordan: Good to loop them in. Mei and David, if you can provide an initial set of network rules and a service account, our SEs can run the hosted baseline with simulated traffic.
[09:38] Mei: We'll share a 7-day sample of request logs and tokenization stats. Expect that by 2025-03-24.
[09:45] [10:00] Alex: Timeline — we want to make a deployment decision in 6 weeks. Is that realistic?
[10:06] Jordan: Yes. Week 1: onboarding and data collection. Week 2: hosted baseline run. Weeks 3-4: dedicated sizing and deeper stress tests. Week 5: analysis and cost comparison. Week 6: decision and SOW sign-off. That's a 6-week plan.
[10:24] Samira: We should also include an acceptance criteria checklist for the POC: latency thresholds, cost delta threshold vs current, and reliability metrics during the spike.
[10:36] Mei: Can you be explicit on acceptance criteria? Example: p50 < 120ms and p95 < 400ms for 80% of steady-state traffic, less than 5% error rate, and cost per 1M tokens no more than 20% above our current infra baseline.
[10:52] Priya: We'll capture those as part of the POC success matrix and report them after each test.
[11:04] [12:00] Jordan: Quick question on data residency — do you need a private instance only for EU-bound data or across the board?
[11:12] Alex: Only EU-bound payment and health vertical flows require strict residency. We might route sensitive classes to Private and keep other traffic on Hosted or Dedicated.
[11:22] Samira: That's a common hybrid approach — policy-based routing: sensitive flows to Private, general flows to Hosted/Dedicated. We can demonstrate routing policies in the PoC.
[11:36] David: For Private, how much lead time to provision on-prem vs VPC?
[11:42] Priya: VPC Private (cloud-hosted VPC with customer networking) generally 2–4 weeks depending on approvals; on-prem depends heavily on site readiness and can be 6–12 weeks. We'll include both timelines in the SOW.
[11:58] Mei: Security team will want to see the architecture diagram and a runbook for incident response.
[12:05] Jordan: We'll share the architecture diagram and an incident response template.
[12:12] [20:00] Sophie: What about integration complexity — do you provide SDKs and sample code for retry/backoff and token management?
[12:20] Samira: Yes, we have SDKs in Python, Node, and Java; also examples for best practices for batching and token budgeting. We'll share a repo link. The SDKs support streaming, function calling, and structured outputs.
[12:36] Alex: Any gotchas with the model catalog? We want to keep vendor flexibility and avoid lock-in.
[12:42] Priya: Redwood supports multiple open models and curated model variants; you can pin model versions and we support automatic fallback to smaller variants on capacity issues. That helps avoid tight lock-in.
[12:58] Mei: For the benchmark harness — will you run cost comparisons using real tokenization from our data?
[13:04] Samira: Yes we'll run tokenization on your sample prompts to get accurate token counts and cost estimates.
[13:12] David: Network egress — any unexpected bandwidth charges we should expect?
[13:18] Jordan: For Hosted, outbound egress will follow cloud provider rates which we can estimate; Dedicated and Private options can reduce egress if colocated. We'll show egress estimates in cost matrix.
[13:30] [24:00] Alex: Are there reference customers that have similar promo spike profiles?
[13:36] Jordan: We have a couple of retailers who've run similar promos; we can share anonymized performance patterns and a short case study.
[13:44] Sophie: I'd like to see an example case where you used prefix caching to reduce token costs.
[13:50] Samira: We'll include a short note and bench scenario demonstrating prefix caching benefits at 50% hit rate.
[14:01] Mei: One more technical — how do you measure tail latencies when batching increases with load?
[14:07] Samira: The runtime collects per-request latencies and batch size distributions; we produce p50/p90/p95/p99 by sequence length and by batch size. That will be in the benchmark report.
[14:24] [36:00] Priya: Quick note on quantization: for some 13B/70B variants we recommend 4-bit quantization profiles that yield 20–40% speedups with small quality deltas. We'll recommend a quant profile per model with sample evals.
[14:42] Mei: We'll want to see quality regression tests as part of the POC — automated evals on our prompt set.
[14:49] Samira: Yes we'll run rouge/bertscore-style regressions plus domain-specific metrics you provide.
[15:00] [44:00] Alex: Suppose the hosted run is good for latency and cost — what's the migration path to Dedicated? How long to flip traffic?
[15:06] Jordan: Migration path is straightforward: you can pin to a Dedicated model endpoint and do a canary rollout. We support traffic splitting, canary policy, and automatic fallback. Provisioning Dedicated GPUs may take 2–10 days depending on capacity.
[15:22] David: Will there be downtime during cutover?
[15:25] Samira: No — cutovers are designed to be zero-downtime with traffic split and warm-up strategies. We'll validate during the POC.
[15:36] Sophie: Any legal items we should start now? NDA amendments or data processing agreements?
[15:42] Jordan: We'll attach the security pack and the data processing addendum; legal review typically takes a couple of weeks. We'll surface the core items for your legal team.
[15:55] [55:00] Jordan: Last part — recap and explicit next steps. We will: send SOW and cost comparison by 2025-03-26, Samira will send benchmark spreadsheet and harness links, Tidewave will upload sample traffic by 2025-03-24, and we'll schedule the hosted baseline week of 2025-03-31.
[15:58] Alex: Sounds good. Any objections to that plan?
[16:02] Mei: No objections. We'll get the artifacts out.
[16:10] Sophie: Thanks, looking forward to the numbers.
[16:12] Jordan: Great, we'll follow up with calendar invites for bench kickoff and internal E2E playbook. Thanks everyone.
